card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility synergy in eutectic high-entropy alloys be improved by inheriting the composite lamellar nature through tailored thermo-mechanical processing?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Arc-melting followed by suction-casting into a copper mold, multi-pass cold-rolling to 84–86% reduction in thickness, and non-isothermal annealing at 660, 700, 740, or 900 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests with an initial strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4 s−1 using dog-bone specimens (15 mm gauge length, 3.2 mm width, 600 μm thickness) and loading–unloading–reloading (LUR) tests.. Findings: The DPHL700 and DPHL740 samples achieved a yield strength of approximately 1.5 GPa with an elongation of ~16%, representing a simultaneous enhancement in both strength and ductility compared to as-cast and ultrafine-grained counterparts.; The microstructure exhibited a two-hierarchical heterogeneity consisting of submicron-grade FCC/B2 grains within FCC lamellae and micron-grade alternate FCC/B2 lamellae.; The average diameters of FCC and B2 grains were roughly comparable at ~0.71 μm, with inter-lamella spacings ranging from 1.5 to 5 μm.; Phase decomposition resulted in two types of NiAl-rich precipitates in FCC lamellae: small intragranular P1 grains (50–180 nm) and large intergranular P2 grains (~350 nm).; Back-stress measurements at the yield point reached ~950 MPa, which was approximately 3 times higher than the effective stress, primarily responsible for the high yield strength.; The strain-hardening rate (Θ) showed a transient behavior with an up-turn in region II and sustained high Θ over a wide strain region III for DPHL700.; Microcrack-arresting mechanisms were observed where multiple microcracks were inhibited from coalescing, with ductile components acting as efficient crack arresters.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced properties to a two-hierarchical constraint effect that generates long-range back-stress by storing geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) due to strain gradients at lamella interfaces and around intergranular precipitates, combined with a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism where the aligned lamellar architecture delays crack propagation and coalescence.. Limitations: The authors note that while the DPHL structure is effective, increasing the annealing temperature to 900 °C induced a partially degraded lamellar structure that led to inferior tensile properties, indicating the sensitivity of the process to thermal treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that further efforts should be devoted to exploring non-equiatomic alloys and spinodal decomposition to create low-misfit coherent nanostructures for even higher yield strengths, and anticipate modifying the EHEA to satisfy requirements for high-temperature and/or corrosion environments.. Quote: "The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism."

W2150567030.title: Heterogeneous lamella structure unites ultrafine-grain strength with coarse-grain ductility

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

W2622849719.title: Phase‐Transformation Ductilization of Brittle High‐Entropy Alloys via Metastability Engineering

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys be designed to achieve ultra-high strength while retaining good ductility, overcoming the limitation of near-equiatomic compositions that restrict the formation of high-volume fractions of ductile strengthening precipitates?. System: Al0.5Cr0.9FeNi2.5V0.2 (non-equiatomic, ~50 at% Ni, ~18 at% Cr, ~4 at% V). Processing: Arc-melting pure metals, casting into copper mold, solution-treating at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by water quenching, cold-rolling with 72% reduction ratio, and ageing at 600 °C or 700 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 on dog-bone-shaped samples (gauge length 10 mm, width 3 mm, thickness 1 mm).. Findings: Achieved an ultrahigh yield strength of 1810 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1905 MPa in the sample aged at 600 °C.; The strength increment relative to the solution-treated sample was >1500 MPa (>560%).; Retained good ductility with elongation of ~9–10% after achieving the maximum strength.; Formed high-content ordered L12 nanoprecipitates with a volume fraction of ~50.1% in the 600 A sample.; The L12 phases are coherent with the FCC matrix, with a lattice parameter difference of only 0.0001 nm (0.3582 nm vs 0.3583 nm).; The spinodal nanostructure contributed 1158 MPa to the yield strength, while grain boundaries contributed 212 MPa.; The total estimated yield strength increase (1524 MPa) agrees closely with the experimental result (1536 MPa).; The mean diameter of the ordered L12 precipitates was determined to be ~35 nm.. Mechanism: The alloying strategy utilizes spinodal decomposition to create a low-misfit coherent nanostructure where the L12 nanophases resist dislocation motion by providing strong diffuse attractive obstacles to trap moving dislocations and by creating antiphase boundaries (APBs) on the slip planes when sheared by dislocations. The diffuse coherent interfaces minimize elastic strain accumulation, preventing crack initiation and maintaining ductility.. Limitations: The authors note that the calculated strengthening contributions based on assuming spherical precipitates may underestimate the area of APBs and the strengthening effect because the actual L12 phases are irregular and interconnected. Additionally, the volume fraction calculations may not be absolutely precise.. Future work: The authors anticipate that this alloying strategy can offer more possibilities for the compositional design of HEAs and will open new avenues for development of ultrastrong and ductile HEAs superior to existing commercial alloys, potentially competing with traditional structural materials in rigorous service conditions.. Quote: "Here we present a strategy to design ultrastrong HEAs with high-content nanoprecipitates by phase separation, which can generate a near-equiatomic matrix in situ while forming strengthening phases"

card: Paper card. Question: How can a single-phase face-centered cubic medium-entropy alloy achieve both gigapascal yield strength and high uniform ductility without relying on second-phase heterogeneities?. System: Equimolar CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (33.48Cr-32.46Co-34.06Ni atomic percent). Processing: Electromagnetic levitation melting, homogenization at 1,473 K for 12 h, hot forging (1,323–1,173 K), cold rolling to 0.5 mm sheets, followed by partial recrystallization annealing at 873 K for 1 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, room temperature (298 K) and liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K); loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests to measure back stresses. Findings: Yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1,150 MPa achieved with a three-level heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nanometer to micrometer scales.; Uniform tensile strain (Eu) reached 22% at room temperature, significantly higher than the ~2% Eu observed in homogeneous ultrafine-grained counterparts with similar strength.; The number density of nanograins (ρNG) increased from 4.7 grains/µm² before testing to 21 grains/µm² after deformation at 298 K and 31 grains/µm² at 77 K.; Back stress hardening accounted for over 80% of the total stress elevation observed during strain hardening from yield to ultimate tensile stress.; The strain hardening rate (Θ) exhibited a distinct upturn between 4% and 8% strain, contrasting with the monotonic drop seen in homogeneous structures.; The width of hysteresis loops in LUR tests was the largest ever recorded for any known alloy, indicating exceptionally high internal back stresses.; Corner twins evolved into nanograins during tensile straining, dynamically reinforcing the heterogeneity of the grain structure.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous grain structure induces load partitioning and strain gradient hardening, causing dislocation pile-ups at grain boundaries and generating geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). This creates large long-range internal back stresses that sustain strain hardening. Additionally, the low stacking fault energy facilitates the dynamic generation of twinned nanograins at grain boundaries during deformation, which further refines the structure and perpetuates back stress hardening.. Limitations: The beneficial effects of the HGS diminish if the material undergoes extended annealing toward uniform grains or if the alloy has high stacking fault energy where full dislocations dominate and recover/annihilate easily.. Future work: The authors propose that this strategy is generally applicable to other single-phase low-SFE alloys and metals to achieve simultaneous high yield strength and high tensile ductility.. Quote: "This heterogeneity results from this alloy's low stacking fault energy, which facilitates corner twins in recrystallization and stores deformation twins and stacking faults during tensile straining."

card: Paper card. Question: How can cryo-rolling and annealing be utilized to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in multiphase high entropy alloys, specifically regarding the development of a hierarchical microstructure?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Multi-pass cryo-rolling up to ~90% reduction in thickness with immersion in liquid N2 for 45 minutes before and after each pass, followed by annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile tests at ambient temperature with an initial strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1; Nano-indentation with load increased linearly from 1 μN to 500 μN over 0.25 seconds.. Findings: The cryo-rolled and annealed material achieved a Yield Strength (YS) of 1437 ± 26 MPa and Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) of 1562 ± 33 MPa.; The elongation to failure (ef) was approximately 14 ± 1%, which remained almost unchanged compared to the as-cast material (17 ± 1%).; The hierarchical microstructure consists of fine lamellar regions with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and coarse non-lamellar regions with coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm).; The hardness of the B2 phase (~12 GPa) is nearly three times higher than that of the L12 phase (~4 GPa) in the as-cast material.; The cryo-rolled and annealed material covers the entire hardness spectrum with softer regions (≤8 GPa), intermediate regions (~8–12 GPa), and much harder regions (≥12 GPa).; The cold-rolled and annealed material showed a homogenous microduplex morphology with grain sizes of ~0.5 µm, unlike the heterogeneous cryo-rolled structure.; The cryo-rolled and annealed EHEA possesses the highest YS and UTS while maintaining appreciable ductility compared to other HEAs like Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi and Fe40Mn27Ni26Co5Cr2.. Mechanism: The simultaneous enhancement in strength and ductility originates from a characteristic hierarchical microstructure that creates profuse domain boundaries separating domains of different hardness, leading to significant back stress strengthening and delayed necking due to strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs).. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%)"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the miscibility gap in bimetallic Co-Mo alloys be overcome to create tunable, highly active catalysts for ammonia decomposition using earth-abundant elements?. System: Quinary CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 where x + y = 70) and control samples of bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru. Processing: Carbothermal shock technique involving flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon nanofibers; temperature reached 2000–2300 K with ramping rates on the order of 10^5 K s−1 and shock duration of ~55 ms. Test conditions: Ammonia decomposition in a plug flow reactor at 250–600 °C using 5 vol% NH3 (and 100 vol% NH3 for specific tests) at a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 36 L gcat−1 h−1. Findings: HEA-Co25Mo45 achieved a mass-specific reaction rate of 22.1 gNH3 gmetals−1 h−1 at 500 °C, representing an improvement factor of ~19 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~3 versus Ru.; The most active catalyst, HEA-Co25Mo45, reached 50% NH3 conversion (T50) at 422 °C, compared to 600 °C for Ru and 600 °C for bimetallic Co-Mo.; The apparent activation energy (Eapp) varied from 64.7 kJ mol−1 for the most active HEA-Co25Mo45 to 123.1 kJ mol−1 for the least active HEA-Co55Mo15.; Nitrogen desorption energy (ΔEN) for HEA-Co25Mo45 was ~79 kJ mol−1, which is very close to the value for Ru (84 kJ mol−1).; Catalytic activity exhibited a volcano-type behavior with respect to nitrogen adsorption energy, peaking at an optimal ΔEN of ~79 kJ mol−1.; The HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst showed negligible degradation after ~50 hours of continuous operation at 500 °C.; For pure NH3 decomposition, HEA-Co55Mo15 achieved an improvement factor of ~118 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~40 versus Ru.; Atomistic modeling confirmed a single solid-solution phase with δ = 5.4% and ΔHmix = 0.65 kJ mol−1, showing no phase segregation up to 1000 K.. Mechanism: The high catalytic activity is attributed to the robust tuning of surface nitrogen binding strength via the Co/Mo ratio; the optimal activity arises from a tradeoff where Co-rich catalysts bind N too weakly (limiting dehydrogenation) and Mo-rich catalysts bind N too strongly (limiting N2 desorption), with the HEA composition allowing access to the optimal intermediate binding energy (~79 kJ mol−1) predicted by the Sabatier principle.. Limitations: The text notes that the peak intensities in XRD patterns are low due to the much smaller particle sizes compared to previously reported HEAs, and that the bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts are constrained by large miscibility gaps in their phase diagram.. Future work: The authors propose designing practical reactors with cascaded catalyst layers having gradually changing nitrogen binding strengths to match the varying concentration of NH3 along the flow, which can be readily achieved by varying the Co/Mo ratios in HEA catalysts.. Quote: "Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a single-phase face-centered-cubic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy be fabricated via 3D ink-extrusion using inexpensive blended oxide nanopowders followed by co-reduction and sintering, and what are the resulting microstructural and mechanical properties?. System: Co3O4 + Cr2O3 + Fe2O3 + NiO blended oxide nanopowders (target composition: 25Co-25Cr-25Fe-25Ni at.%), poly-lactic-co-glycolic-acid binder, dibutyl phthalate plasticizer, ethylene glycol butyl ether surfactant. Processing: 3D ink-extrusion printing of oxide-polymer ink using nozzles of 200–510 µm diameter; de-binding at 150 °C and 300 °C for 30 min each; co-reduction and sintering in flowing H2 (99.999%, 250 ml min−1) at 1557–1573 K for 1 h with heating rate of 10 K min−1. Test conditions: Tensile testing of single filaments (125 µm diameter, 10 mm gauge length) at 293 K and 130 K; compressive testing of micro-lattices (solid volume fractions 25–63%) at 77 K and 293 K; in situ synchrotron XRD in flowing H2 (1.3 ml min−1, 19.9 keV) from room temperature to 1215 K. Findings: Final relative density achieved is 99.6 ± 0.1% after sintering at 1573 K for 1 h, with porosity of 0.4 ± 0.1%.; Strut diameters as low as 103 µm were produced using a 200 µm nozzle, demonstrating isotropic shrinkage of 78% in volume.; Tensile yield strength at 293 K is 250 ± 5 MPa with ultimate tensile strength of 598 ± 8 MPa and fracture strain of 33.8 ± 1.3%.; At 130 K, yield strength increases to 388 ± 7 MPa, ultimate tensile strength to 864 ± 12 MPa, and fracture strain to 37.6 ± 0.7%.; In situ XRD reveals sequential reduction: Co, Fe, and Ni form rapidly between 573–673 K, while Cr2O3 reduction begins above 1073 K.; Final microstructure consists of equiaxed grains sized 5 to 25 µm containing annealing twins.; Average coefficient of thermal expansion calculated as 21.6 ± 0.5 × 10–6 K−1 between 293 and 1215 K.; Micro-lattices show no catastrophic cracking up to 50% strain, with stress increasing continuously due to stretching-dominated plastic deformation.. Mechanism: The process relies on the rapid sequential reduction of Co3O4, Fe2O3, and NiO to form metallic Co, Fe, and Ni, which initiate densification. Cr2O3 reduces slowly above 1073 K, and the resulting Cr diffuses into the Co-Fe-Ni matrix, forming a single-phase fcc CoCrFeNi alloy. The isotropic and homogeneous shrinkage during co-reduction and sintering preserves the printed architecture despite a 78% volume reduction, while the small initial agglomerate size (<10 µm) and high surface area enable fast reaction kinetics and near-full density.. Limitations: Residual sub-micrometer porosity and swelling voids remain after sintering; the measured yield stress is lower than bulk values due to the small number of grains (2–3) across the filament diameter; larger unreduced Cr2O3 particles can act as diffusion barriers and sintering inhibitors, leading to local encapsulation.. Future work: Hot isostatic pressing could be applied to eliminate residual closed porosity; the method allows for compositional flexibility to create compositionally-graded HEAs or combinatorial alloy discovery; the technique can be scaled for high-volume production of lightweight, high-ductility structures operating from liquid nitrogen up to ~1000 °C; miniaturization to sub-micron scale lattices could push mechanical performance limits.. Quote: "A complex phase evolution path is observed by in-situ X-ray diffraction in extruded filaments when the oxide phases undergo reduction and the resulting metals inter-diffuse, ultimately forming face-centered-cubic equiatomic CoCrFeNi alloy."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the rapid solidification inherent to additive manufacturing (specifically SLM and DLF) influence phase selection, microstructure, and mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional processing methods?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) / Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) defined as having at least five principal elements in equimolar/equiatomic compositions (5%–35% concentration each); specifically discussed in the context of bulk HEAs processed by SLM, SEBM, and DLF.. Processing: Additive manufacturing techniques including Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM), and Direct Laser Fabrication (DLF); DLF allows the use of elemental powders fed from different hoppers to produce in situ chemically homogeneous alloys, avoiding the need for pre-alloyed powders.. Test conditions: Not stated in the provided text; the text is a review summarizing published data rather than reporting new experimental test conditions for specific HEA samples.. Findings: HEAs are particularly well suited to AM, with the field expected to grow significantly in the coming years.; Laser-induced rapid solidification in AM can avoid compositional segregation and restrict the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds.; AM of HEAs allows the use of elemental powders as feedstock in DLF, avoiding the need for pre-alloyed metal powders.; Rapid solidification inherent to AM provides a tool to aid phase selection during alloy fabrication.; Traditionally, arc-melting requires extensive re-melting and intermittent ingot inversions, while SPS requires powder alloying and refinement via ball milling.; AM offers advantages over traditional methods by addressing shape and size limitations of HEA components.; The configurational entropy in HEAs stabilizes simple solid solutions (bcc, fcc, hcp), but competition with enthalpy often dictates the final microstructure.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the rapid solidification inherent to the AM process restricts the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds and avoids compositional segregation, while the high configurational entropy stabilizes simple solid solution phases. In DLF specifically, the mechanism involves the controlled supply of elemental powders from different hoppers to produce chemically homogeneous alloys in situ under optimized processing conditions.. Limitations: The text notes that AM of HEAs is a nascent field, stating that 'only two papers on SEBM and SLM' had been published at the time of writing, and that the properties obtained and effects of processing on microstructures are still being discussed.. Future work: The authors state that 'we may expect this field to grow significantly in the coming years' and that the properties and microstructural effects of AM on HEAs are currently being discussed, implying a need for further characterization of these relationships.. Quote: "The impact of rapid solidification inherent to AM on phase selection is highlighted for high-entropy alloys."

Paper card. Question: How does the use of LENS™ additive manufacturing influence the microstructure, phase constitution, and mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys compared to conventional casting, and can it enable the creation of compositionally graded materials?. System: Al1.5CoCrCuFeNi, ZrTiVCrFeNi, TiZrNbMoV, AlCoCrCuFeNiTi, AlCoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.3, 0.6, 0.85), AlxFeCoCrNi(2-x) (x = 0.3, 1), AlxCuCrFeNi2 (0 < x < 1.5), AlCrSiTiV, Al2CoCrCuFeNi. Processing: Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS™) using powder-fed systems with elemental powder blends or pre-alloyed powders; Laser cladding with laser power 0.4–3 kW, beam size 0.6–4.5 mm, scanning velocity 1.7–12 mm/s, and effective energy 46–208 J/mm²; Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM) using gas-atomized powder; Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using gas-atomized powder. Test conditions: Compression testing, tensile testing, microhardness testing, magnetic property measurement (saturation magnetization and coercivity), dry sliding wear tests at room temperature and 500°C, hydrogen storage exposure, annealing exposure. Findings: LENS™ processing of Al1.5CoCrCuFeNi resulted in dendritic grains containing an ordered B2 structure and a disordered bcc matrix, avoiding the slow cooling and segregation typical of arc-melting.; ZrTiVCrFeNi and TiZrNbMoV alloys synthesized via LENS™ exhibited dendritic two-phase structures and performed well for hydrogen storage due to non-equilibrium solute-trapping effects.; SLM CoCrFeNi achieved a yield strength of 600 MPa, triple that of its cast equivalent (188 MPa), while maintaining high ductility (32% elongation).; SEBM-processed AlCoCrFeNi showed superior ductility (14%–26% elongation) compared to the as-cast state (5% elongation), attributed to grain refinement and the presence of an fcc phase.; In AlxCuCrFeNi2 graded deposits, microhardness increased progressively with Al content as the microstructure transitioned from fcc/L12 to bcc/B2.; Magnetic properties varied with Al content: low Al regions were weakly ferromagnetic, while high Al bcc/B2 regions were strongly ferromagnetic with high saturation magnetization.; Laser-cladded HEA coatings achieved room temperature hardness values exceeding ceramic particle-reinforced Mg-, Al-, and Ti-matrix alloys and Nb, Ta, and Mo alloys.; AlCrSiTiV clad coatings showed a friction coefficient of ~0.3 and specific wear rate of ~2.10⁻⁵ mm³/Nm, which were 2 and 3 times lower than the Ti-6Al-4V substrate, respectively.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the observed microstructural changes and property enhancements to the rapid cooling rates (10⁴–10⁶ K/s) inherent to laser-based additive manufacturing, which cause significant grain refinement, non-equilibrium solute-trapping, and the formation of non-equilibrium phases like bcc that are favored over fcc. The high temperature gradients and solidification rates control the columnar-to-equiaxed transition, while the high viscosity and sluggish diffusion rates of HEA melts limit dilution with substrates.. Limitations: The text notes that the statistical comparison of phases in laser-cladded coatings is biased because 90% of reported coatings contain Al, which stabilizes the bcc phase. Additionally, the presence of metallurgical defects, heterogeneity, and anisotropy in microstructures limits the use of these techniques for fracture applications, and durability properties like corrosion resistance and fracture toughness require further characterization.. Future work: The authors propose that systematic efforts must be made to characterize powder characteristics more finely and incorporate these into simulations. They suggest implementing tools to characterize materials in real-time during processing and using advanced techniques like synchrotron diffraction. Further focus should be devoted to evaluating microstructure and tensile properties to understand the mechanisms of microstructure development, and to exploring in situ thermal treatments to design multiphase steel architectures.. Quote: "The faster cooling rates obtained via direct laser metal deposition lead to a significant non-equilibrium solute-trapping effect, which in turn avoided the component segregation and relieved the solubility limitations."

W1995781421.title: Structure and hydrogen storage properties of a high entropy ZrTiVCrFeNi alloy synthesized using Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS)

card: Paper card. Question: Does hydrogen exposure cause catastrophic failure (hydrogen embrittlement) or can it improve mechanical properties in an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of pure elements (Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 at.%), hot-rolling at 900 °C (50% reduction), homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h, water-quenching, cold-rolling (60% reduction), and annealing at 900 °C for 3 min followed by water-quenching.. Test conditions: Electrochemical hydrogen charging in 0.1 M NaOH + 0.05 g·L−1 CH4N2S at pH = 13 and 25 °C; pre-charging durations of 12 h (15 mA·cm−2), 72 h (25 mA·cm−2), and 240 h (100 mA·cm−2); in-situ tensile testing at a rate of 1 × 10−4 S−1 with continuous charging.. Findings: The hydrogen-free alloy exhibited an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 545 MPa and total elongation of ~68%.; Pre-charging for 12 h at 15 mA·cm−2 (8.01 wt.ppm H) increased UTS to 571 MPa and uniform elongation to ~71%.; Pre-charging for 72 h at 25 mA·cm−2 (15.22 wt.ppm H) increased UTS to 588 MPa and uniform elongation to ~71%, representing ~7.9% and ~4.4% increases over the hydrogen-free sample.; Pre-charging for 240 h at 100 mA·cm−2 (33.25 wt.ppm H) showed a slightly reduced increment in strength and ductility compared to the 15.22 wt.ppm sample, suggesting saturation.; Hydrogen alloying did not exert significant effects on the yield strength of the alloy.; The hydrogen alloyed HEA with 15.22 wt.ppm H exhibited the highest strain-hardening rate among all conditions.; The density of deformation nanotwins significantly increased in hydrogen alloyed samples compared to the hydrogen-free alloy.; The intrinsic stacking fault energy of the alloy is ~19 mJ·m2, which is reduced further by hydrogen.. Mechanism: Hydrogen reduces the stacking fault energy and phase stability of the f.c.c. lattice, which triggers more intense nanotwinning upon loading. This increased nanotwin density enhances the work-hardening rate via the 'dynamic Hall-Petch' effect (continuous grain fragmentation and reduced dislocation mean free path), thereby simultaneously increasing strength and ductility. At very high hydrogen concentrations, unfavorable mechanisms like hydrogen enhanced localized plasticity or surface cracking compete with the beneficial twinning, leading to saturation or slight reduction in gains.. Limitations: The text notes that at the highest hydrogen concentration (33.25 wt.ppm), the increment in strength and ductility was reduced, likely due to a competition between beneficial nanotwining and unfavorable mechanisms like hydrogen enhanced localized plasticity or initial surface cracks caused by high surface hydrogen concentration.. Future work: The authors propose that these results open new pathways for the design of strong, ductile, and hydrogen tolerant materials by utilizing hydrogen to tune beneficial hardening mechanisms rather than viewing it solely as a harmful impurity.. Quote: "hydrogen in an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) leads not to catastrophic weakening, but instead increases both, its strength and ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a new half-Heusler type high-entropy alloy be synthesized to achieve simultaneous increases in Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity, and how does nanostructuring via ball milling duration affect its thermoelectric performance?. System: Ti2NiCoSnSb (High-Entropy Alloy). Processing: Vacuum arc melting (VAM) followed by ball milling (BM) for 1 h (microcrystalline) or 5 h (nanocrystalline) using toluene as process control agent at 300 rpm, consolidated by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1373 K for 5 min under 50 MPa pressure.. Test conditions: Thermoelectric properties measured from room temperature to 873 K; thermal diffusivity measured via laser flash technique.. Findings: The 1 h BM-SPS (microcrystalline) sample achieved a power factor of 1.02 mWm−1K−2 at 860 K.; The 5 h BM-SPS (nanocrystalline) sample achieved a power factor of 0.57 mWm−1K−2 at 860 K.; The microcrystalline alloy exhibited a ZT of 0.144 at 860 K.; The nanocrystalline alloy exhibited a ZT of 0.047 at 860 K.; The nanocrystalline alloy showed a simultaneous increase in Seebeck coefficient (37 µV/K to 72 µV/K) and electrical conductivity (1.08 × 10^5 Sm−1 at RT) with increasing temperature.; The microcrystalline alloy showed a Seebeck coefficient increase from 60 µV/K to 120 µV/K between room temperature and 860 K.; The 5 h BM-SPS sample contained 11% TiC secondary phase, while the 1 h BM-SPS sample contained 5% TiC.; The 1 h BM-SPS sample exhibited a total thermal conductivity similar to bulk TiNiSn, whereas the nanocrystalline alloy showed an increase in thermal conductivity with temperature.. Mechanism: The simultaneous increase in S and σ in the nanocrystalline sample is attributed to preferential scattering of majority carriers at the increased number of interfaces (varying from ~15 nm to 2 μm) in the nanocrystalline structure. The lower ZT in the nanocrystalline sample compared to the microcrystalline sample is due to the higher volume fraction of TiC and Ni3Sn4 secondary phases, which increase electrical conductivity but also significantly raise thermal conductivity, thereby reducing the overall figure of merit.. Limitations: The formation of secondary phases (TiC and Ni3Sn4) during SPS, caused by carbon pick-up from toluene during ball milling, destabilizes the HH phase and limits the ZT value. The ZT values obtained (0.144 and 0.047) are lower than those of pure TiNiSn, although higher than TiCoSb.. Future work: The authors state that the effect of the high-entropy (HE) effect on thermoelectric properties is in the nascent stage of understanding and is a subject for further study.. Quote: "Nanostructuring leads to simultaneous increase in S and σ with increasing temperature."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of B4C and the variation of starting particle sizes of solvent (TaC) versus solute (HfC, Mo2C, TiC) carbides influence the phase evolution, crystal structure transformation, and mechanical properties of refractory high-entropy ceramic composites synthesized via pulsed current processing?. System: Quaternary (HfC, Mo2C, TaC, TiC) and Quinary (HfC, Mo2C, TaC, TiC, B4C) high-entropy carbide composites. Processing: Pulsed current processing (Spark Plasma Sintering) at 1800 °C for 5 min under vacuum with a uniaxial pressure of 60 MPa and a heating rate of 100 °C/min. Test conditions: Microstructure and phase identification via SEM (15 kV), EDS, and XRD (5–120° 2 Theta); nanohardness measured with a Berkovich indenter at 100 mN load and ambient temperature. Findings: The quaternary (4-HEC) composite formed two FCC phases: a Ta-rich phase (0.4429 nm) and a high-entropy phase (0.4399 nm) with a hardness of 28.4 GPa.; Adding B4C induced a transformation from FCC to a hexagonal structure in the high-entropy phase with higher solute content (HEC2), while a lower-content phase (HEC1) retained the FCC structure.; The addition of B4C delayed the sintering shrinkage temperature range from 1000–1600 °C (4-HEC) to 1370–1690 °C (5-HEC), indicating hindered atomic diffusion.; Reducing the particle size of solute carbides (HfC, Mo2C, TiC) promoted interdiffusion, resulting in a higher fraction of the hexagonal structured HEC phase compared to using larger particles.; Tuning the particle size of the solvent carbide (TaC) had a negligible effect on the final phase composition.; Reducing TaC particle size from −325 mesh to <1 µm increased the nanohardness of the composite from 21.4 GPa to 23.1 GPa.; The HEC(fine) composite (finest solute particles) showed a Young's modulus of 401 GPa, an improvement over the 380.7 GPa observed in the HEC(+) composite.. Mechanism: TaC acts as the solvent carbide due to its low metal vacancy formation energy; constituent atoms diffuse into TaC vacancies causing lattice distortion. The addition of B4C promotes the diffusion of B atoms, which have longer bond lengths than C atoms, inducing severe lattice distortion that transforms the FCC structure to hexagonal. Reducing solute particle size shortens diffusion distances, enhancing the kinetics of phase transformation toward the hexagonal structure.. Limitations: The study notes that EDS lacks accuracy for quantitative analysis of light elements, and the presence of porosity in some samples complicated the nanoindentation testing, requiring matrix indentations to obtain bulk property averages.. Future work: The authors state that a detailed investigation on the sintering behavior of ceramic precursors to form high-entropy ceramic composites will be reported later, elsewhere.. Quote: "The high entropy phase and Ta-rich phase displayed a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure with similar lattice parameters, suggesting that TaC acted as a solvent carbide during phase evolution."
W2943555138.title: Processing and Characterization of Refractory Quaternary and Quinary High-Entropy Carbide Composite

card: Paper card. Question: Can configurational entropy be engineered to stabilize a single-phase solid solution in a five-component oxide system where the constituent binary oxides do not form solid solutions, and can this transition be reversed?. System: Equimolar mixture of MgO, CoO, NiO, CuO, and ZnO (labeled E1). Processing: Solid-state synthesis: powders milled for 2 h, pressed into pellets at 31,000 N, fired in air at temperatures ranging from 700 to 1,100 °C with 50 °C increments, and quenched; thin films prepared via pulsed laser deposition at 600 °C with 3 J cm⁻² energy density.. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring phase evolution from 700 to 1,100 °C; differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ XRD at 5 °C min⁻¹; EXAFS at Advanced Photon Source 12-BM-B; STEM-EDS analysis at 200 kV.. Findings: Full conversion to a single-phase rocksalt structure occurs between 850 and 900 °C, with no additional peaks observed above this range.; Removing any single component from the five-component mixture results in a multiphase material when equilibrated at 875 °C for 12 h.; Deviations from equimolarity by ±2, ±6, and ±10% increase the transition temperature to single phase, confirming the entropic driving force.; The phase transformation from multiphase to single phase is endothermic, with a measured enthalpy change of approximately 12 kJ mol⁻¹ (±2 kJ mol⁻¹).; EXAFS data shows cation-to-anion first-neighbour distances are identical within ±0.01 Å for Zn, Ni, Cu, and Co, consistent with random distribution.; STEM-EDS mapping reveals chemically and structurally homogeneous material with no evidence of phase separation or clustering at the atomic scale.; A small mass loss of approximately 1.5% occurs at the transition due to the reduction of 3+ to 2+ cations during the conversion of spinel intermediates to rocksalt.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high configurational entropy of the five-component equimolar mixture overcomes the positive enthalpic penalties associated with structural transitions (specifically for CuO and ZnO) and mixing, stabilizing the single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. The entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy becomes dominant, driving the reversible transition from a multiphase state to a random solid solution where cations occupy a single sublattice homogeneously.. Limitations: The authors note that quantitative calorimetry presents challenges, and the assumption of ideal mixing for enthalpy calculations is a simplification; literature reports indicate finite and mixed-sign enthalpies of mixing that are not fully captured by the reference transition enthalpy values.. Future work: The authors propose that entropic stabilization should be explored in other systems with intermediate anions, such as chalcogenides, nitrides, and halides, particularly where covalent character is modest, and call for rigorous theoretical exploration of the crystallographic model where intermediate anions render cation sites energetically equivalent.. Quote: "entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy solid solutions be formed in non-oxide ceramic metal diborides with a hexagonal layered structure, and do they exhibit superior hardness and oxidation resistance compared to their constituent individual diborides?. System: Seven equimolar five-component metal diborides: (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Mo0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Mo0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Cr0.2Ti0.2)B2, and (Hf0.2Zr0.2W0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2. Processing: High-energy ball milling (HEBM) for 6 hours in WC media with 60-minute milling/5-minute cooling cycles, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under 30 MPa pressure in vacuum (10^-2 Torr). Test conditions: Hardness measured via Vickers indentation at 200 kgf/mm2 with 15s hold time; oxidation resistance assessed via sequential isothermal annealing in flowing dry air at 800–1500 °C for 1 hour per step. Findings: Six of the seven compositions formed a single-phase hexagonal AlB2 structure with greater than 92% of theoretical density.; Aberration-corrected STEM confirmed 2-D high-entropy metal layers separated by rigid boron nets with no detectable layered segregation along the c-axis.; The measured standard deviations of lattice spacings between basal (0001) planes were only ~0.6% of the average c lattice parameter.; Hardness of the high-entropy diborides was generally greater than the average hardness of the five individual constituent metal diborides.; Oxidation resistance was generally better than the average of individual components, with HEB#1 and HEB#7 maintaining shape at 1500 °C while TiB2 pulverized.; Revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factors based on lattice constants (δc) of 3.9% to 5.2% rationalized single-phase formation, whereas the non-single-phase specimen had δc ≈ 6.2%.; Minor secondary oxide phases ((Zr, Hf)O2) were observed in six specimens, and a secondary (Ti1.6W2.4)B4 phase was found in the W-containing specimen.. Mechanism: The formation of high-entropy solid solutions is rationalized by a revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factor calculated from lattice constants rather than atomic radii; the rigid 2-D boron net constrains the metal layers, reducing the effective size mismatch (δa) and allowing entropy stabilization of the disordered solid solution despite larger atomic size differences in the c-direction.. Limitations: The presence of porosity and oxide inclusions resulting from the HEBM procedure adversely affected hardness and oxidation resistance; MoB2 is metastable at room temperature and W2B5 starting powder has limited solubility; the study did not fully optimize microstructure for maximum property performance.. Future work: Further systematic investigation of hardness, oxidation resistance, and other properties is needed, particularly focusing on processing optimization to achieve fully-dense and oxide-free specimens and utilizing the large compositional design space to tailor protective oxide scales.. Quote: "Greater than 92% of the theoretical densities have been generally achieved with largely uniform compositions from nanoscale to microscale."

card: Paper card. Question: Can bulk equiatomic high-entropy carbides be synthesized from UHTC monocarbides, and what factors govern single-phase solid solution formation and mechanical property enhancement?. System: Equiatomic (Hf-Ta-Zr-Ti)C and (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high entropy Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic (UHTC) carbides; constituent monocarbides HfC, TaC, ZrC, NbC, TiC; binary (Hf-Ta)C. Processing: Ball milling of equiatomic precursor powders (200 rpm, 24 hr, WC pots, SiC media, stearic acid, 5:1 ball-to-powder ratio) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2300 °C under 16-40 MPa; optimized route included a degassing step (1800 °C, 10 min) and a 7 min dwell at 2300 °C. Test conditions: Nanoindentation testing using an Agilent/Keysight G200 Nanoindenter with a diamond Berkovich tip, Continuous Stiffness Measuring (CSM) mode, maximum penetration depth of 300 nm, strain rate of 0.05 s−1, and 64 indents per sample. Findings: The (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C composition achieved 99% density and single-phase homogeneity with the optimized processing route, whereas (Hf-Ta-Zr-Ti)C showed incomplete diffusion of ZrC.; The optimized (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high entropy carbide exhibited a hardness of 36.1 ± 1.6 GPa, significantly higher than the hardest monocarbide (HfC, 31.5 ± 1.3 GPa) and the binary (Hf-Ta)C (32.9 ± 1.8 GPa).; A relative enhancement in hardness of approximately 30% was observed compared to the rule of mixtures value (27.7 GPa) calculated from the component monocarbides.; Chemical decomposition was observed in the center of samples sintered for 10 min at 2300 °C, indicating the presence of a miscibility gap in the (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C system.; The lattice parameter mismatch of the component monocarbides was identified as a key factor for predicting single-phase solid solution formation, analogous to the Hume-Rothery atomic size misfit parameter.; The indentation modulus showed a moderate increase from ZrC through HfC~(Hf-Ta)C and TaC~NbC to the (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high entropy carbide.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the enhanced hardness arises from solid solution hardening effects caused by local non-uniformities in the lattice structure (localised strains) that impede dislocation motion, or from interesting bonding behavior leading to enhanced elastic constants; they also suggest that lattice parameter mismatch influences diffusion kinetics and solid solution formation.. Limitations: The direct comparison between measured hardness and rule of mixtures calculated hardness is not quantitatively valid without knowing the dominant room temperature slip system of the high entropy carbide; the thermal conductivity of the high entropy phase is unknown, and the mechanism for the observed miscibility gap requires further modeling.. Future work: The authors state they are undertaking ongoing future work to study the hardness behavior, specifically to test the theory regarding low thermal conductivity and to understand the miscibility behavior through further modeling studies and thermal conductivity measurements.. Quote: "revealing a significantly enhanced hardness (36.1 ± 1.6 GPa,) compared to the hardest monocarbide (HfC, 31.5 ± 1.3 GPa)"

card: Paper card. Question: What is the microstructural stability of the AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr refractory metal high-entropy superalloy following long-duration thermal exposures at elevated temperatures?. System: AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr (20Al–10Mo–20Nb–10Ta–20Ti–20Zr at.%). Processing: Arc melting of elemental metals (≥99.9% purity) under inert Ar atmosphere, inverted and re-melted five times, homogenised at 1400 °C for 24 h, furnace cooled to 750 °C at 10 °C/min then to room temperature; long duration thermal exposures of 1000 h at 1200, 1000, and 800 °C in Ta foil wrapped quartz tubes under vacuum, followed by quenching into ice water.. Test conditions: 1000 h exposures at 1200 °C, 1000 °C, and 800 °C; microstructural characterisation via SEM, EDX, and XRD.. Findings: The initial nanoscale cuboidal B2 + bcc microstructure was found to be unstable following thermal exposures at all tested temperatures.; Extensive intragranular precipitation of a hexagonal Al-Zr-rich intermetallic occurred at 1200, 1000, and 800 °C.; At 1200 °C, the volume fraction of the Al-Zr intermetallic precipitates approached 50%.; At 1200 °C, the B2 phase was absent, indicating the material was in a two-phase field of bcc and hexagonal intermetallic.; At temperatures ≤1000 °C, the alloy existed in a three-phase field comprising bcc, B2, and hexagonal intermetallic phases.; The increased Zr content in AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr resulted in approximately double the volume fraction of Al-Zr intermetallic compared to AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr0.5 at 1200 °C.; Thermodynamic predictions using various databases showed significant deviations from experimental findings, particularly regarding the stability range of the B2 phase and Al-Zr intermetallics.. Mechanism: The formation of the nanoscale B2 + bcc microstructure is driven by a miscibility gap between Zr and refractory metals; however, extensive precipitation of the Al-Zr intermetallic depletes the matrix of Al and Zr, stabilizing a bcc structure and preventing B2 formation at high temperatures. The B2 phase forms during cooling from a bcc precursor via spinodal decomposition plus ordering.. Limitations: The authors state that thermodynamic databases currently do not offer high fidelity for predicting phase equilibria in these systems, and the B2 phase was not predicted by many databases or only at temperatures below 900 °C, contrary to experimental observations at 1000 °C.. Future work: Further experimental studies of phase equilibria are required to assess microstructural stability and provide data to refine thermodynamic databases for better predictive capability in RSA systems.. Quote: "Crucially, the initial nanoscale cuboidal B2 + bcc microstructure was found to be unstable following the thermal exposures."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the number of principal elements (N) in equimolar multi-principal element alloys affect the probability of forming disordered solid solution (SS) phases versus intermetallic (IM) phases, and what are the implications for high-temperature structural applications?. System: Equimolar combinations of 3 to 6 elements from a palette of 26 metallic elements (including Al, Si, Mo, Ta, W, Nb, Ti, V, Re, Zr, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, etc.). Processing: High-throughput computational screening using the CALPHAD method (Pandat v.8.1 software) to calculate phase diagrams for 134,547 equimolar alloy systems; results filtered for credibility where the fraction of fully assessed binary systems (fAB) equals 1.. Test conditions: Phase diagrams calculated between 600 °C and 3,600 °C; properties evaluated at the solidus temperature (Tm) and at 600 °C; maximum use temperature (Tuse) estimated as the lowest of 0.8Tm or the last first-order phase reaction temperature below Tm.. Findings: The fraction of solid solution (SS) alloys decreases as the number of elements (N) increases: at Tm, 30% of 3-component alloys are SS, dropping to only 5% for 6-component alloys.; Configurational entropy rises slowly with N (as ln(N)), while the number of binary interactions increases rapidly (as (N/2)(N−1)), explaining why IM formation becomes more probable as N increases.; The maximum solidus temperature (Tm) decreases with N: 2,925 °C for 3-component, 2,754 °C for 4-component, 2,435 °C for 5-component, and 2,056 °C for 6-component alloys.; The maximum maximum use temperature (Tuse) decreases with N: 2,285 °C for 3-component, 1,846 °C for 4-component, 1,677 °C for 5-component, and 1,159 °C for 6-component alloys.; Only 3 out of 209 SS alloys with Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C are 6-component alloys, whereas 108 are 3-component alloys.; Extreme property values (highest/lowest density, modulus, cost) are achieved in ternary (3-component) alloys, while 6-component alloys show tighter property spreads.; 51 equimolar alloy systems with 3 ≤ N ≤ 5 were identified that satisfy aggressive design criteria (Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C, density ≤ 10 g cm−3, modulus ≥ 100 GPa, cost ≤ $200/kg, no IM phases at Tm).. Mechanism: The authors argue that while configurational entropy (Smix) favors solid solution stability, it increases only logarithmically with the number of elements. Conversely, the number of binary element pairs increases quadratically, raising the probability that at least one pair has a sufficiently large negative formation enthalpy (Hf) to overcome the entropy term in the Gibbs free energy equation (G = H - TS), thereby stabilizing intermetallic phases.. Limitations: The study is restricted to equimolar compositions; non-equimolar alloys were not explored and may offer higher Tm or Tuse values. Additionally, the credibility filter (fAB=1) excluded over 95% of the calculated systems, potentially missing viable alloys if less stringent criteria were acceptable.. card: Paper card. Question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?. System: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr (Refractory High Entropy Alloy). Processing: 1. Vacuum/argon arc melting followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 2 hours under 210 MPa argon. 2. Homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 hours followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature (Condition 1). 3. Solutionizing Condition 1 at 1400 °C for 20 min followed by water quenching (Condition 2). 4. Annealing Condition 2 at 600 °C for 120 hrs followed by water quenching (Condition 3).. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) and 600 °C uniaxial compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001 s−1; Vickers microhardness (4.9 N load, 15 s dwell); Microstructural characterization via SEM, TEM, and Atom Probe Tomography (APT).. Findings: Condition (1) (continuous B2 matrix) exhibited a yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compressive strain before fracture.; Condition (2) (single-phase weakly ordered BCC) showed high ductility with no fracture after 60% true strain but lower yield strength (1065 MPa).; Condition (3) (inverted microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates in continuous BCC matrix) achieved a yield strength of 1345 MPa and 16.9% peak strain with fracture at 38% strain.; At 600 °C, Condition (3) showed anomalous strengthening with a yield strength of 1423 MPa (higher than its RT value of 1345 MPa) and 16.2% plasticity.; APT analysis revealed strong elemental partitioning: B2 phase is rich in Al and Zr, while BCC phase is rich in Nb and Ta.; The microstructure of Condition (3) consists of discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm) within a continuous disordered BCC matrix, contrasting with Condition (1) where B2 is the continuous matrix.; Condition (1) hardness was 562 ± 16 HV, Condition (2) was 405 ± 11 HV, and Condition (3) was 475 ± 12 HV.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the poor ductility in Condition (1) is caused by the continuous ordered B2 matrix, which is inherently brittle. The improved ductility in Condition (3) is attributed to the 'inversion' of the microstructure, where the continuous phase becomes the more ductile disordered BCC matrix, while the hard B2 phase exists as discrete precipitates providing strengthening. The anomalous strengthening at 600 °C in Condition (3) is speculated to result from competing slip systems in the complex B2 phase (e.g., <001>{110} and <111>{112}) leading to sessile kinks or dislocation debris, similar to mechanisms in Ni3Al.. Limitations: The authors state that the details of the strengthening mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study and that the explanation for the anomalous strengthening at 600 °C is highly speculative. They note that applying classical precipitation hardening models requires parameters (lattice misfit, elastic properties, fault energies) that are difficult to quantify in this complex RHEA.. Future work: The authors recommend additional scientific studies to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions on precipitation strengthening parameters, further investigation of deformation mechanisms at room temperature and 600 °C, and additional studies at higher temperatures and under tensile loading.. card: Paper card. Question: How do the microstructure, phase formation, and corrosion properties of AlCrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy coatings differ when prepared by high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) versus high-velocity air fuel (HVAF) thermal spraying?. System: Equimolar AlCrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (feedstock produced by inert gas atomization). Processing: Thermal spraying using HVOF (K2 liquid-fueled system) and HVAF (M3TM-HVAF system with 4L4C nozzle, 250 mm length, 22.75 mm exit diameter) on mild steel substrates (EN 1.0045) grit blasted at 2.5 bar, 70° angle; HVOF used -45 +15 µm powder, HVAF used -33 +15 µm powder. Test conditions: Potentiodynamic polarization in 0.5 M NaCl and 0.05 M H2SO4 aerated electrolytes at room temperature; surface interrupted at 2 mA/cm2 for microscopy; microhardness HV 0.1; roughness Ra, Rz; porosity via optical microscopy. Findings: Porosity reduced from 0.6 ± 0.2% in HVOF coatings to 0.3 ± 0.1% in HVAF coatings; Microhardness increased from 600 ± 50 HV 0.1 (HVOF) to 680 ± 20 HV 0.1 (HVAF); Surface roughness decreased from Ra: 4.6 ± 0.1 µm (HVOF) to Ra: 4.0 ± 0.2 µm (HVAF); Corrosion current density (icorr) reduced by a factor of two in HVAF coatings compared to HVOF in NaCl electrolyte; Passivation current density in H2SO4 reduced to 0.013 mA/cm2 for HVAF vs. 0.073 mA/cm2 for HVOF; Pitting potential remained similar for both coatings (947 mV for HVOF vs. 957 mV for HVAF); No distinct oxide lamellae formed in HVAF coatings due to reduced thermal input; Metastable bcc (B2) structure retained in both coating types with lattice parameter a = 2.87 Å. Mechanism: The reduced thermal input in HVAF spraying suppresses oxygen pick-up and oxide formation, leading to lower porosity and a denser microstructure. The finer powder fraction used in HVAF results in decreased grain size and increased hardness. The improved corrosion resistance and passivation behavior in HVAF coatings are attributed to the formation of a denser and more protective passive layer, likely due to the reduced structural defects and lower oxide content.. Limitations: No passivation was observed in either coating type when tested in 0.5 M NaCl electrolyte; extensive delamination and coating failure occurred at high current densities in NaCl; the study was limited to as-sprayed conditions without post-deposition heat treatment.. Future work: The authors state that the HVAF process shows high potential for processing HEAs and imply further investigation into optimizing parameters for even better defect reduction and corrosion resistance, though specific future experiments are not detailed beyond the general potential of the process.. Quote: "Precipitation reactions are suppressed by the rapid solidification during atomization and by the relatively low thermal input during spraying."

W2754629136.title: Microstructure and Wear Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiTi High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Produced by HVOF

card: Paper card. Question: What is the influence of titanium content (molar ratios x = 0.0 to 1.5) on the microstructure, phase formation, and wear behavior of the AlCoCrFeNiTix high-entropy alloy system?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTix with molar ratios x = 0.0; 0.2; 0.5; 0.8; 1.0; 1.5. Processing: Arc-melting of elemental granules (≥99.9% purity) in a water-cooled copper crucible under argon atmosphere (1.1 bar, 2 × 10−4 mbar base pressure), remelted three times with turning for homogeneity; cooling rate <50 K/s. Test conditions: Microhardness (HV0.5, 10 indents), XRD (Co Kα, 20°–130° 2θ), DSC (1800 K to room temperature, 20 K/min cooling), ball-on-disk, oscillating wear, and scratch tests; reference material: bearing steel EN 1.3505. Findings: The alloy without titanium (x = 0.0) exhibits a homogeneous microstructure with a single chemically ordered bcc (B2) phase and an average microhardness of 550 HV0.5.; Alloying with titanium causes the formation of two major bcc phases (ordered B2 and disordered A2) and increases microstructural heterogeneity.; For x ≥ 0.5, a minor face-centred cubic (fcc) phase forms in the cell walls, and for x = 0.8, a tetragonal σ phase is detected.; Microhardness increases with titanium content, reaching a maximum of 770 HV0.5 for the equimolar composition (x = 1.0), then decreases to 730 HV0.5 for x = 1.5 due to porosity.; The alloy AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 shows superior wear resistance in ball-on-disk tests with the lowest wear depth compared to other compositions and bearing steel.; Under oscillating wear conditions, the alloy with x = 0.5 has the lowest wear depth, but all HEAs exhibit higher wear depth (lower resistance) than the bearing steel.; Samples with x ≥ 0.8 exhibit spalling and secondary cracks under abrasive conditions due to the formation of complex phases (tetragonal, cc, hexagonal Laves) that reduce ductility.. Mechanism: Titanium's large atomic radius causes solid solution strengthening and shifts lattice parameters, while its addition stabilizes a second disordered bcc phase and promotes the formation of complex intermetallic phases (fcc, σ, cc, Laves) at higher concentrations. These complex phases increase hardness but reduce ductility by possessing low numbers of slip systems, leading to brittle behavior and spalling under abrasive loads.. Limitations: The authors note that the formation of the σ phase is sensitive to manufacturing conditions and can be dissolved by heat treatment. Additionally, for the highest titanium content (x = 1.5), cavities and shrinkage porosity caused by different phase contraction reduced microhardness and may have influenced wear results.. Future work: The authors propose that AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 is a promising candidate for wear protection applications in both bulk and coating materials, suggesting further investigation into its potential for such uses.. Quote: "Alloying with titanium showed strong influence on the resulting microstructure and lead to an increase of microstructural heterogeneity."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the power of atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) influence the microstructure, frictional wear resistance, and corrosion resistance of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings?. System: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings (HEACs) on low carbon steel (45#) substrates. Processing: Atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using mechanically milled powders (15–50 μm) with four power levels (H1 < H2 < H3 < H4); H4 utilized the highest hydrogen-gas flow rate and power. Test conditions: Tribological tests: Si3N4 ball (5 mm), 5 N load, 1200 s sliding time; Corrosion tests: 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, room temperature, 240 h immersion, potentiodynamic polarization, EIS (100 kHz–10 MHz). Findings: Volume fractions of pores decreased from 4.31 ± 0.90% (H1) to 0.59 ± 0.12% (H4) as APS power increased.; The H4 coating achieved the lowest coefficient of friction (COF) of 0.38 ± 0.08, indicating the best wear resistance.; H4 coating exhibited the highest corrosion potential and lowest corrosion current density among all samples.; Impedance modulus |Z| at 0.1 Hz for H4 was ~1459 Ω·cm², significantly higher than H1 (~382 Ω·cm²).; The H4 coating thickness was 80 ± 8 μm, showing significantly higher deposition efficiency than H1 (56 ± 6 μm).; Oxygen content in wear trace regions (delamination, debris, etc.) for H4 ranged from 14.27 to 20.22 at. %.; The passive film on H4 contained bound water (H2O) at 532.5 eV, which helps assemble dissolving metal ions.. Mechanism: Increased APS power enhances the melting rate and alloying process, reducing porosity and improving coating density. During wear, multi-component metal oxides form and flake off to create a lubricating layer that prevents severe adhesion wear. For corrosion, the dense microstructure and the presence of bound water in the passive film (composed of Cr/Fe oxides) enhance protection against pitting initiation by Cl− ions.. Limitations: The text notes that excessive gas flow in intermediate power settings (H1-H3) caused rapid cooling, leading to uneven melting and high porosity; also, the H4 coating still exhibited some pitting corrosion at phase boundaries after 240 h immersion.. Future work: The authors state that by changing processing parameters, it is feasible to acquire an AlCoCrFeNi HEAC with both excellent wear resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance, implying further optimization of APS parameters is viable.. Quote: "The frictional wear and corrosion resistance of the coating are simultaneously improved with an increase of the power of APS."

card: Paper card. Question: Is it feasible to produce the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via in-situ alloy formation using laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) from elemental powders, and how do process parameters influence defect formation, microstructure, and phase composition?. System: W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 (refractory metal high entropy alloy) fabricated from a heterogeneous mixture of elemental W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V powders.. Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) using an AconityMINI machine with a 1 kW fiber laser (1080 nm) on a Mo substrate in Argon atmosphere (<25 ppm O2). Two parameter sets were used: Set A (600 W, 800 mm/s, 120 µm hatch, 125 J/mm³) and Set B (100 W, 100 mm/s, 45 µm hatch, 889 J/mm³). Vanadium powder content was increased by a factor of 1.5 to compensate for evaporation.. Test conditions: Samples (6 × 6 × 6 mm³) were analyzed via optical microscopy, SEM, EBSD, TEM, and microhardness testing. Microhardness was measured as HV0.1. Cooling rates are estimated at 10⁶ K/s.. Findings: Relative densities reached 99.8% for parameter set A and 99.5% for parameter set B.; A single bcc-phase was confirmed by EBSD and TEM, consistent with vacuum arc melted samples.; Average grain size was 16.3 µm for PBF-LB/M B, which is more than four times smaller than the 80 µm reported for vacuum arc melted samples.; Parameter set B (higher volumetric energy density) resulted in fewer undissolved tungsten particles compared to set A.; Parameter set A exhibited smaller cracks than set B, which showed wider cracks due to higher internal stress.; Microhardness of the coarser structure (Set A) was 561 ± 17 HV0.1, while the finer cellular structure (Set B) was 614 ± 21 HV0.1.; Elemental segregation was observed: V concentrated in interdendritic areas, while W and Ta were predominantly in intradendritic areas.; Solidification mode shifted from dendritic (Set A) to cellular (Set B) based on growth rate (R) and temperature gradient (G) conditions.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the formation of undissolved W particles to the high melting point of tungsten, which requires high volumetric energy input and slow scan speeds to dissolve. Cracking is caused by internal stresses from the PBF-LB/M process combined with the alloy's low room temperature ductility and brittle grain boundaries (likely due to O and N impurities). The microstructure (dendritic vs. cellular) is controlled by the ratio of growth rate (R) to temperature gradient (G), where higher R and lower G favor dendrites, while lower R and higher G favor cellular structures.. Limitations: Samples contained cracks and undissolved tungsten particles; completely defect-free samples were not produced. The study notes that the alloy has limited room temperature ductility and fracture toughness.. Future work: The authors suggest using a high-temperature (>600 °C) build-platform heating device and/or high-purity powder with low O and N content to achieve crack-free processing. They also propose verifying if more recently developed refractory metal high entropy alloys with increased room temperature ductility can be processed without high-temperature heating.. Quote: "The relative density of the samples with a dimension of 6 × 6 × 6 mm3 reaches, in dependence of the PBF-LB/M parameter set, 99.8%."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM (HITACHI SU-8010) and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance tested via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning voltage −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Findings: A single BCC solid solution was formed without secondary phases, with an experimental lattice parameter of 3.2034 Å.; Elements with lower melting points and densities (Nb and Mo) showed negative molar ratio deviations of up to 3.5% (Nb: −3.5 at%, Mo: −0.16 at%) compared to the nominal 25%.; The average grain size was 13.4 μm, significantly smaller than the 200 μm observed in as-cast NbMoTaW HEA.; Primary and secondary dendrite arm spacings were 6.59 μm and 1.68 μm, respectively, much finer than the 20–30 μm spacing in as-cast samples.; The average microhardness of the SLM-fabricated sample reached 826 Hv, compared to 446 Hv for arc-melted HEA and 310–437 Hv for superalloys.; The free-corrosion current (Icorr) of the NbMoTaW HEA was 8.716 × 10−11 A, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of 316 L steel (8.815 × 10−9 A).; Visual corrosion testing showed 316 L steel suffered up to 1 mm corrosion depth, while the NbMoTaW alloy exhibited only crack extension and minor pitting.. Mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM creates extremely high temperature gradients and cooling rates, limiting growth time and resulting in fine grains and slender dendrites. Composition deviations occur because powders with lower melting points and densities fuse first, spread over larger areas, absorb more energy, and evaporate earlier during the process. The improved hardness is attributed to grain refinement following the Hall–Petch law, while superior corrosion resistance is due to the presence of easily passivating elements (Nb, Mo, Ta) despite minor segregation.. Limitations: The ductility of the NbMoTaW HEA at room temperature remains low, and while composition deviation exists (up to 3.5%), it is noted that further study of mechanical properties is still necessary.. Future work: Further study of mechanical properties is required to fully assess the potential of the SLM-fabricated NbMoTaW HEA.. Quote: "The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys."

Question: How does varying tungsten concentration affect the crystal structure, microstructure, and mechanical properties (hardness, strength, ductility) of WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys fabricated via laser cladding deposition?. System: WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys with x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53 (mole fractions). Processing: Laser cladding deposition (LCD) using a coaxial LCD system with 565 W laser power, 8 mm/s scanning speed, 0.08 mm layer thickness, and 600 °C induction heating temperature; powders (45–125 μm) mixed for 4 h and dried at 120 °C for 8 h in Argon (<80 ppm O2). Test conditions: Vickers microhardness (500 g load, 30 s); room temperature compression (25 °C, 0.001 s⁻¹); high-temperature compression (1000 °C, 3.5 min heating, 15 min soak, 0.001 s⁻¹ strain rate, 10⁻³ torr vacuum). Findings: All WxNbMoTa alloys formed a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution regardless of tungsten content.; Grain and dendrite sizes averaged 20 μm and 4 μm, respectively, due to rapid solidification in LCD.; Vickers microhardness increased with tungsten concentration: 459.2 ± 9.7, 476.0 ± 12.9, 485.3 ± 8.7, and 497.6 ± 5.6 Hv for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; NbMoTa (x = 0) exhibited yield strength of 530 MPa and compressive strain of 8.5% at 1000 °C.; At room temperature, NbMoTa showed yield strength of 874 MPa and compressive strain of 5.8%, while W-containing alloys were brittle with compressive strengths of 840–895 MPa.; Bulk modulus increased with tungsten content: 174, 182, 186, and 192 GPa for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; Spherical gas porosities in as-fabricated samples were eliminated by using molybdenum powders with higher granule density and good sphericity.. Mechanism: Rapid solidification during laser cladding deposition (melting in 10⁻³–10⁻² s) suppresses constitutional segregation and promotes fine equiaxed grains. Tungsten addition increases lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening, raising hardness and bulk modulus but reducing ductility at room temperature. Porosity formation is attributed to adsorbed Argon gas in low-density molybdenum powder particles, not microstructure features.. Limitations: Spherical gas porosities appeared in samples fabricated with standard molybdenum powders due to low granule density; tungsten addition reduces room-temperature plasticity, making W-containing alloys brittle.. Future work: The present work provides a theoretical basis for LCD manufacturing of aerospace parts of refractory HEAs with large size, complex structure, and variable composition.. Quote: "The size of the grains and dendrites are 20 μm and 4 μm on average, due to the rapid solidification characteristics of the laser cladding deposition."

card: Paper card. Question: How can optimal process parameters be established for in situ alloying of Ti6Al4V with Cu during Laser Powder Bed Fusion to achieve dense parts with required mechanical properties and antibacterial functionality?. System: Ti6Al4V (ELI) + 1 at % Cu (1.38 wt %) powder mixture. Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M280 machine; laser power 170 W, spot size 80 µm, layer thickness 30 µm (3D) or 60 µm (tracks/layers), scanning speed 0.7–1.3 m/s, hatch distance 70–100 µm, with single scan and rescan strategies. Test conditions: Vickers hardness (200 gf), tensile tests (0.5 mm/min strain rate), SEM-EDS for elemental distribution, EBSD for phase identification, antibacterial testing against E. coli and S. aureus (10^5 CFU/ml, 24 h incubation at 37 °C). Findings: Hardness increased from 383 ± 13 HV0.2 (pure LPBF Ti6Al4V) to 456 ± 20 HV0.2 for the Cu-alloyed material.; Ultimate tensile strength increased from 1243 ± 49 MPa (pure) to 1550 ± 126 MPa for the Cu-alloyed material.; Cu concentration at the surface ranged from 1.05 wt % (0.7 m/s, 70 µm hatch) to 2.31 wt % (1.3 m/s, 100 µm hatch) using single scan.; Rescan strategy removed majority of copper segregations and improved surface quality.; In the bulk, Cu content varied: 1–1.5 wt % in α′-martensite regions, 2–5 wt % at pool boundaries, and up to 35 wt % in dendritic/cellular regions.; Dendritic/cellular regions with >30 wt % Cu exhibited a Ti-cubic (β) structure, while 1–5 wt % Cu regions retained α′-hexagonal structure.; Antibacterial testing showed a one-order-of-magnitude decrease in E. coli growth and a two-order-of-magnitude decrease in S. aureus growth.; Crack nucleation at the surface was associated with regions containing 20–35 wt % Cu, likely corresponding to β-Ti cubic structures.. Mechanism: Segregation of Cu at molten pool boundaries is explained by differences in viscosity and density between molten Cu and Ti6Al4V; Cu has lower viscosity and higher density, causing it to sink and agglomerate near boundaries if convection is insufficient. The formation of β-Ti cubic structure in Cu-rich areas is due to Cu acting as a β-stabilizer alongside V, stabilizing the high-temperature phase down to room temperature under rapid cooling.. Limitations: Complete alloy homogeneity was not achieved in the bulk; surface roughness influenced tensile test results, making mini-samples behave like notch specimens; diffusion was suppressed due to high cooling rates, potentially leading to higher Cu solubility than equilibrium limits.. Future work: Further optimization of manufacturing parameters and heat treatment investigations are required to achieve a homogeneous alloy with tailored mechanical properties; biocompatibility, bioadhesion, and corrosion resistance must be investigated; testing should include emerging pathogens and isolates from failed implants.. Quote: "Segregation of Cu at boundaries of the molten pool, and generally observed inhomogeneity of the LPBF manufactured Ti6Al4V (ELI)-1% Cu alloy, could be explained with respect to properties of the feedstock materials."
